[[File:Jitinsai.JPG|thumb|right|180px|{{ill|Nobori|ja|幟|lt=Banners|lt_ja=幟}} at a jichinsai held mainly by farmers]]
'''Jichinsai''' ({{Lang-ja|地鎮祭}}, also read ''tokoshizume no matsuri''<ref name="setagaya"/>) is a {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|lt=Shinto|lt_ja=神道}} ritual in {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|lt=Japan|lt_ja=日本}} held at the start of {{ill|Civil engineering|ja|土木|lt=civil engineering|lt_ja=土木}} or {{ill|Construction|ja|建築|lt=construction|lt_ja=建築}} work, to pray that the work will go safely.<ref name="setagaya">{{Cite web|url=https://www.city.setagaya.lg.jp/mokuji/bunka/004/001/d00164372_d/fil/aruzidexe30.pdf|title=Arujidē No.30|website=Setagaya City Board of Education|accessdate=2024-01-15}}</ref><ref name=":0">https://archive.today/20230417215042/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8916</ref>{{Efn|Except at {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|lt_ja=伊勢神宮}}, where it takes place after.<ref name=":0" />}} For building work it is a kind of building ritual.<ref name="setagaya"/> The ritual asks the {{ill|Jinushigami|ja|地主神|lt=landlord deity|lt_ja=地主神}} for permission to use the land for building.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Adriana |date=2017-12-12 |title=Before you build: Groundbreaking ceremonies in Japan |url=https://www.rethinktokyo.com/2017/12/12/you-build-groundbreaking-ceremonies-japan/1513022850 |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=REthink Tokyo - Real Estate Information for Buyers and Investors |language=en}}</ref> It is a way to {{ill|Prayer|ja|祈り|lt=pray|lt_ja=祈り}} for safety during the construction. The {{ill|General contractor|ja|ゼネコン|lt=contractor|lt_ja=ゼネコン}} who puts up the building pays for the ceremony, including the {{lang|ja-latn|{{ill|Omiki|ja|御神酒|lt=omiki|lt_ja=御神酒}}}} and {{ill|Tamagushi|ja|玉串|lt=tamagushi|lt_ja=玉串}} offerings; the owner and others involved help with the costs.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Covingtonandsons|title=Supernatural Stuff|url=https://covingtonandsons.com/Category/supernatural-stuff/|access-date=2023-04-18|website=Covington & Sons Tools|date=30 May 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

There are {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|lt=Shinto|lt_ja=神式}} and {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|lt=Buddhist|lt_ja=仏式}} forms.{{Efn|At the dedication of the south gate of Renge-in in {{ill|Tamana, Kumamoto|ja|玉名市|lt=Tamana|lt_ja=玉名市}}, Kumamoto Prefecture, a Shinto groundbreaking and a Buddhist groundbreaking were held one after the other.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rengein.jp/archive/nandaimon/nandaimon-jitinsai.pdf|title=Nandaimon jichinsai ni go-sanka kudasai|website=Renge-in|accessdate=2024-01-15}}</ref>}} Today the Shinto form is the more common. From old times the rite has also been called ''jimatsuri'' (地祭),<ref name="setagaya"/><ref name="motegi">{{Cite web|author=Motegi Sadasumi|url=https://www.jcca.or.jp/kaishi/284/284_toku4.pdf|title=Jichinsai no rekishi to sono igi|trans-title=The history and meaning of the jichinsai|website=Japan Civil Engineering Consultants Association|accessdate=2024-01-15}}</ref> ''shizume-matsuri'' (鎮祭),<ref name="setagaya"/> ''miyaji kamamuru matsuri'' (宮地鎮謝)<ref name="setagaya"/> and ''jihikisai'' (地曳祭).<ref name="setagaya"/> The Buddhist form is sometimes called ''jichinshiki'' or ''anzen kiganjo''.

People set up a {{ill|Himorogi|ja|神籬|lt=himorogi|lt_ja=神籬}} at the site for the ceremony, and a {{ill|Kannushi|ja|神職|lt=Shinto priest|lt_ja=神職}} blesses the land and obtains permission from its {{ill|Jinushigami|ja|地主神|lt=guardian deity|lt_ja=地主神}}.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ji Chin Sai - Ground breaking Ceremony |url=http://www.shinto.nl/ground_breaking.htm |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=www.shinto.nl}}</ref> The ceremony is held before the builders, designers and clients. A wooden platform is set up with an altar in the centre, on which offerings such as rice, sake, fish, vegetables, salt and water are placed. Sometimes sand or salt from the shore near Ise Grand Shrine is used.<ref name=":0" /> Five-coloured silk banners, {{ill|Masakaki|ja|真榊|lt=masakaki|lt_ja=真榊}}, are used in the ritual.

Rites like the jichinsai are also performed outside Japan, in {{ill|South Korea|ja|大韓民国|lt=South Korea|lt_ja=韓国}} and {{ill|Taiwan|ja|台湾|lt=Taiwan|lt_ja=台湾}}.

== History ==
The oldest records are the mentions of ''shizume-matsuri'' (鎮祭) in the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|lt=Nihon Shoki|lt_ja=日本書紀}}'' under the tenth month of the fifth year and the fifth month of the sixth year of Empress Jitō.<ref name="mitome">{{Cite journal |url=https://archives.bukkyo-u.ac.jp/rp-contents/DO/0036/DO00360R049.pdf|author=Mitome Takeshi |title=Kodai jichin no shikkōsha ni tsuite|trans-title=On the performers of ancient groundbreaking rites |journal=Bulletin of the Graduate School, Bukkyo University |issue=36 |date=2008-03 |pages=49–64 }}</ref><ref name="koike">{{Cite web|author=Koike Hiroshi|url=http://www.kyotofu-maibun.or.jp/data/mukashi/pdf/m-p86-87.pdf|title=Jichin no kigen to miyako no jichin|trans-title=The origin of groundbreaking rites and the rites of the capital|website=Kyoto Prefecture Research Center for Archaeological Properties|accessdate=2024-01-15}}</ref> The ''{{ill|Kogo Shūi|ja|古語拾遺|lt=Kogo Shūi|lt_ja=古語拾遺}}'' (807) says that when {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ja|神武天皇|lt=Emperor Jimmu|lt_ja=神武天皇}} set up his capital at Kashihara, the Ikasuri deity (坐摩神) was worshipped; since it describes Ikasuri as the spirit of the great palace ground (''ōmiyadokoro''), groundbreaking rites are thought to have been held for the building of palaces from early times.<ref name="motegi"/>

The setting up of five-coloured ''nusa'' at the centre and the four corners is attributed to the influence of the Chinese theory of {{ill|Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)|ja|五行思想|lt=yin-yang and the five phases|lt_ja=陰陽五行説}}.<ref name="motegi"/> This yin-yang thought is said to have been officially brought from {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済|lt=Baekje|lt_ja=百済}} by {{ill|Gwalleuk|ja|観勒|lt=Kanroku|lt_ja=観勒}} in the tenth year of Suiko ({{ill|602|ja|602年|lt=602|lt_ja=602年}}).<ref name="mitome"/>

Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|lt=separation of Shinto and Buddhism|lt_ja=神仏分離}} of the modern period, kami and buddhas were more mixed, and the officiants were more varied.<ref name="mitome"/>

In the {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|lt=Heian period|lt_ja=平安時代}}, groundbreaking by esoteric Buddhist monks is said to have flourished in place of the {{ill|Onmyōji|ja|陰陽師|lt=onmyōji|lt_ja=陰陽師}}, but one study finds both the esoteric ''anchin-hō'' and the {{ill|Onmyōdō|ja|陰陽道|lt=Onmyōdō|lt_ja=陰陽道}} ''dokōsai'' continuing until the {{ill|Kamakura period|ja|鎌倉時代|lt=Kamakura period|lt_ja=鎌倉時代}}.<ref name="mitome"/>

== Shinto form ==
=== Order of the jichinsai ===
The ritual ground is set facing south, with ''imitake'' (sacred bamboo) at the four corners hung with ''{{ill|Shimenawa|ja|注連縄|lt=shimenawa|lt_ja=注連縄}}''.<ref name="motegi"/>

In former times a dragon pillar (celebration pillar) was set up, and arrows were set towards the north-east (''ushitora'') and south-west (''hitsujisaru'') to pray for the safety of the building work.<ref>''Shibukawa Shishi'', vol. 4 (Shibukawa City, 1984), p. 106.</ref>

The usual order of a Shinto jichinsai is as follows.
; {{ill|Temizu|ja|手水|lt=Temizu|lt_ja=手水}} (てみず, ちょうず)
: Before entering the ritual ground, participants wash their hands, rinse their mouths and purify body and mind, then take their seats.<ref name="motegi"/>
; {{ill|Shubatsu|ja|修祓|lt=Shubatsu|lt_ja=修祓}} (しゅばつ)
: The priest recites the ''haraekotoba'' and then purifies the ritual ground, the offerings, the ''tamagushi'', the chief officiant and assistants, the owner, the builders and the other participants.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Kōshin (降神), the descent of the deity
: The priest recites the words of descent, then calls out "O…" in the ''keihitsu'' cry, announcing the deity's descent to the participants, who bow their heads.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Kensen (献饌), the offerings
: The priest sets out the ''{{ill|Shinsen|ja|神饌|lt=shinsen|lt_ja=神饌}}'' (rice, sake, rice cakes, sea fish, river fish, seaweed, vegetables, fruit, sweets, salt, water and so on).<ref name="motegi"/> Sometimes the sake is placed before the deity beforehand, and taking the lid off its {{ill|Heishi (vessel)|ja|瓶子|lt=heishi|lt_ja=瓶子}} serves as the offering.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Norito sōjō (祝詞奏上)
: The priest recites a ''{{ill|Norito|ja|祝詞|lt=norito|lt_ja=祝詞}}'' praying for the long life of the land and building, the safety of the work and the prosperity of the owner.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Sanku (散供)
: The four corners of the land are purified in the order north-east, south-east, south-west, north-west, and rice, salt, cut paper and sake are offered directly to the ground.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Kusakarisome (草刈初), the first cutting of grass
: Grass is cut with a sacred sickle (''imikama''), usually by the owner.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Ugachizome (穿初), the first digging
: The ground is broken with a sacred hoe (''imikuwa''), usually by the builders.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Burying the ''shizumemono'' (鎮物)
: The ''shizumemono'' (ritual objects) are placed at the centre of the site; usually only the motion is performed at the jichinsai, and they are actually buried during construction.<ref name="motegi"/>
; {{ill|Tamagushi|ja|玉串|lt=Tamagushi|lt_ja=玉串}} hairei (玉串拝礼)
: The chief officiant and assistants, then the owner, the builders and the other participants offer ''tamagushi'' and bow, in that order.<ref name="motegi"/>
; Tessen (撤饌), the removal of the offerings
: The priest takes down the offerings (sometimes putting the lid back on the ''heishi'' serves as the removal).<ref name="motegi"/>
; Shōshin (昇神), the ascent of the deity
: The chief officiant recites the words of ascent and gives the ''keihitsu'' cry to send the deity off.<ref name="motegi"/>
; {{ill|Naorai|ja|直会|lt=Naorai|lt_ja=直会}} (直会)
: The participants move to another place for the ''naorai''.<ref name="motegi"/>

=== Izumo yashiki jichinsai ===
At {{ill|Izumo-taisha|ja|出雲大社|lt=Izumo Taisha|lt_ja=出雲大社}}, a special rite called the "Izumo yashiki jichinsai"{{Sfn|Koike|2015|p=187}} is held, looking to {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主|lt=Ōkuninushi|lt_ja=大国主大神}}, the highest deity of the land, and praying for the peace and firmness of the land. The ''goshindo'' (sacred soil of Izumo Taisha) and ''shizumemono'' are buried at the house,{{Sfn|Koike|2015|p=187}} and talismans are put on the central pillar and the pillars at the four sides; these are called the ''itsuhashira ofuda'' (five-pillar talismans).{{Sfn|Koike|2015|p=187}} The house then comes under the rule of Ōkuninushi, and all ill-omened directions (''kimon''), curses, unlucky directions and hindrances are said to vanish,{{Sfn|Koike|2015|p=187}} so that the household prospers more and more. The rite follows the traditional ritual of Izumo Taisha, with special features such as the threefold recitation of the divine words, the burial of the sacred soil, and four handclaps. In some areas, after the Izumo yashiki rite, a small offering of first fruits called the '''Izumo nengu''' ("Izumo tribute") is made every year.<ref>''Izumo Ōyashirokyō Fukyōshi Yōsei Kōshūkai'' (Izumo Ōyashirokyō Kyōmu Honchō, 1 September 1989).</ref> Originally the rite was only for Izumo parishioners;{{Sfn|Koike|2015|p=187}} today it is also performed for people coming from other prefectures.{{Sfn|Koike|2015|p=187}}

== Buddhist form ==
In Buddhism it is called ''jichin-hō'' or ''chintaku-hō'' (地鎮法, 鎮宅法), ''anchin-hō'' (安鎮法, short for ''anchin kokka fudō-hō''), ''jitenku'' (地天供), or popularly ''jimatsuri'' or ''jigatame no hō''.{{citation needed|date=January 2024}}

== Tsu Jichinsai Lawsuit ==
In the {{ill|Tsu Jichinsai lawsuit|ja|津地鎮祭訴訟|lt=Tsu Jichinsai lawsuit|lt_ja=津地鎮祭訴訟}} of 1971 the rite was declared secular.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Details of 1971 (Gyo-Tsu) 69 {{!}} Judgments of the Supreme Court |url=https://www.courts.go.jp/app/hanrei_en/detail?id=51 |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=www.courts.go.jp}}</ref>
